notes: “For three ... and for four” is a repeated escalating formula. The following offenses are not a checklist of exactly four items. “I will not turn it back” retains the unstated object, understood in context as judgment.
“Inhabitant” may refer especially to a ruler. Verse 15 follows the pointed “their king”; the consonants can also evoke the Ammonite deity Milcom.
vocabulary: Threshing sledge
A heavy implement used to separate grain; the iron-sledge image makes the violence against Gilead concrete.
Covenant of brothers
An alliance described in the language of kinship and mutual obligation.

notes: The first line’s Hebrew is difficult and may evoke craving the dust on the poor or trampling them into it. The woman in the next line is called a young woman, not explicitly a prostitute; the shared access by father and son remains unsoftened.
Pledged garments are collateral taken from debtors; fines supply the wine. The loaded-cart verb in verse 13 is rare and may describe pressing down or creaking under weight.
vocabulary: Nazirite
A person under a special vow of dedication, which includes abstaining from wine.
Fruit and roots
The tree image spans above and below to portray complete destruction.

notes: “Known” describes a special relationship, not lack of awareness of other peoples. The meeting in verse 3 need not imply agreement on every belief or aim.

The tiny remains recovered from a lion make “rescue” bitterly ironic. The final couch phrase is obscure; this draft retains Damascus rather than presenting a reconstructed furniture description as certain.
vocabulary: Store up
Normally used of treasures; here what fills the citadels is violence and plunder.
Altar horns
Projections at the altar’s corners, here broken off and thrown down.

notes: The feminine forms address women through the insulting image “cows of Bashan.” The terms rendered hooks have other proposed meanings, and Harmon is an uncertain destination. The captive women’s humiliation is retained.
The commands are sarcastic: more worship accompanies more rebellion. “Every three days” follows the text rather than changing it to the three-year tithe schedule elsewhere.
“His thought” may concern God’s thought or a human being’s thought. The Hebrew does not fully resolve the pronoun.
vocabulary: Clean teeth
An image of having nothing to eat, explained by the parallel lack of bread.
Return
The unchanged refrain links five episodes of distress to the people’s failure to respond.

notes: Gilgal’s name echoes the Hebrew for going into exile. Bethel, “house of God,” is said to become aven, worthlessness or trouble.

The wilderness question and the tense of carrying the images are debated. Sikkuth and Kiyyun follow the pinned Hebrew; other ancient forms underlie later quotations. “Beyond Damascus” is retained rather than harmonized to “beyond Babylon.”
vocabulary: Gate
The civic place where disputes and legal business were heard.
Stream that never runs dry
The image contrasts enduring justice with unreliable or seasonal flow.

notes: The comparison’s pronouns in verse 2 are not fully explicit. The body-burning term in verse 10 is rare. Verse 12 follows the pinned “oxen”; a different division of the consonants yields plowing the sea.
Lo-debar sounds like “nothing,” and Karnaim means “horns.” The place-names also expose the boast in their own strength.
vocabulary: Joseph
A collective ancestral name for the people whose ruin is ignored by the revelers.
Wadi
A valley or stream channel, which may carry seasonal water.

notes: Anak is traditionally rendered “plumb line,” but its exact material and meaning are uncertain. The draft keeps that established image while marking the uncertainty.

Amaziah reports a threat against Jeroboam himself, whereas verse 9 names his house. Amos’s verbless denial can be read “I am” or “I was” no prophet. “Prophet’s son” can refer to membership in a prophetic group rather than biological parentage.
The oracle explicitly includes sexual humiliation, the deaths of sons and daughters, land seizure, and exile. It does not explain the wife’s circumstances or imply freely chosen prostitution.
vocabulary: King’s mowing
A harvest taken before the later growth; the vision specifies this vulnerable agricultural moment.
Sycamore figs
Fruit of the sycamore-fig tree, distinct from the tree commonly called sycamore in some English-speaking regions.

notes: Summer fruit, qayits, sounds like “end,” qets. The building in verse 3 can be a temple or palace; the terse final “Hush!” is retained.

“Pride of Jacob” is an ambiguous oath expression. “Samaria’s Guilt” and “the way of Beer-sheba” are difficult religious references; proposed deity names or pilgrimage interpretations should not be mistaken for explicit wording.
vocabulary: Ephah; shekel
A measure of grain and a weight used for payment. Shrinking one and enlarging the other cheats the buyer twice.
Famine of hearing
The announced scarcity is of hearing the LORD’s words, not merely of food or possession of texts.

notes: The heavenly chambers and vault preserve the poem’s architectural imagery. Tseror in verse 9 can mean a pebble or small solid piece; interpreting it as grain changes how the sieve image is heard.

The pinned Hebrew has “possess” and “Edom.” The Greek wording reflected in Acts has a different reading involving humanity and seeking. This draft preserves the Hebrew source rather than harmonizing the passages.
vocabulary: Caphtor; Kir
Places named in the Philistine and Aramean origin traditions here; the verse places their migrations beside Israel’s departure from Egypt.
Shelter
Sukkah: a booth or shelter, used here for David’s fallen rule rather than replaced with “palace.”
